title: Now Is the Day of Salvation: Open Hearts and a Holy Temple
summary: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain, since now is the day of salvation. He commends his ministry not by credentials but by endurance through hardship, by character, and by the Spirit, in a long series of paradoxes: dying yet alive, sorrowful yet rejoicing, poor yet making many rich. He asks them to open their hearts to him, and then warns them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for they are the temple of the living God.
story: Chapter 5 ended with Paul, as Christ's ambassador, pleading with people to be reconciled to God. Chapter 6 presses the appeal on the Corinthians themselves, who have received grace but whose relationship with Paul, and perhaps with God, is strained. The chapter's first half completes Paul's description of his ministry by listing what it has cost him. Its second half is personal: he has opened his heart to them and asks them to do the same. The warning of 6:14-7:1 about partnership with unbelievers then interrupts, before Paul returns to the plea to make room in their hearts in 7:2.
historical:
The hardships in verses 4-5 correspond to events recorded in Acts and in Paul's own letters: beatings and imprisonment at Philippi (Acts 16:22-24), riots at Ephesus and elsewhere (Acts 19:23-41), and long labor with his own hands to support himself (Acts 20:34; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). Chapter 11 gives a fuller account.

The passage 6:14-7:1 is one of the most debated in the letter. It seems to break the flow, since 6:13 ("Open wide your hearts also") reads naturally into 7:2 ("Make room for us in your hearts"). It also uses several words found nowhere else in Paul, including Belial, and some scholars have noted similarities to the language of the Dead Sea Scrolls. For these reasons some consider it a fragment of another letter, possibly the earlier letter mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5:9, or a non-Pauline piece inserted later. Others defend it as Paul's own, placed deliberately: the Corinthians' continued ties to pagan temples and the influence of false apostles were exactly what was keeping their hearts closed to him. The Greek manuscripts all include it in this position.
cultural:
Corinth was full of temples, and much of its social life, from trade guild meals to family celebrations, took place in their dining rooms with food offered to the gods. First Corinthians 8-10 had already addressed whether believers could eat in such settings; Paul's answer was that they must not take part in idol worship (1 Corinthians 10:14-22). The questions of verse 16, "What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols?", would have had concrete meaning for them.

The image of being "unequally yoked" comes from farming. Deuteronomy 22:10 forbade plowing with an ox and a donkey together, animals of different strength and kind that cannot pull as one. Paul applies the picture to partnerships that bind believers to unbelief in ways that compromise their loyalty to Christ. Belial, in verse 15, comes from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness, used in the Old Testament for scoundrels (for example, in Deuteronomy 13:13); by Paul's time Jewish writings, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, used it as a name for Satan, the prince of evil.
literary: Verse 2 quotes Isaiah 49:8, from the second of the Servant Songs, and applies it to the present moment: "now is the day of salvation". Verses 4-10 are among the most rhetorically crafted lines Paul wrote. They move from a list of hardships (verses 4-5), to a list of virtues and spiritual resources (verses 6-7), to a string of paradoxes built on "yet" (verses 8-10), where the world's view of the apostles and the truth about them are set side by side. The chapter then turns intimate, with Paul addressing the readers by name, "Corinthians", which he rarely does, and calling them his children. The closing section (verses 14-18) is a series of rhetorical questions followed by a chain of Old Testament quotations woven together from several passages, including Leviticus 26:12, Ezekiel 37:27, Isaiah 52:11, and 2 Samuel 7:14.

outline.t: Do not receive God's grace in vain
Ministry commended through hardship and paradox
Our hearts are open wide; open yours
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers
Come out and be separate: the promises of God

doctrines.note: Paul applies Isaiah's promise of a time of favor to the present: "now is the day of salvation". Salvation is God's gift in Christ, yet it can be received "in vain", as a grace heard but not allowed to shape life. The urgency is not manufactured; it arises from the fact that God's time of favor has arrived.

Believers are called to separation not from people but from idolatry and whatever defiles, because they belong to God. Holiness here is the consequence of a promise: God will dwell among them and be their Father. The passage continues into 7:1, "perfecting holiness in the fear of God".

"We are the temple of the living God" (verse 16). The church as a community, not only the individual believer, is the place where God dwells, fulfilling the Old Testament promise that God would live among his people.

words.note: Kairos, time, especially a fitting or decisive moment, as distinct from chronos, time as duration. Isaiah's "time of favor" is a kairos, and Paul declares that it is now. The word gives the appeal of verse 2 its urgency.

Heterozygeo, to be yoked with a different kind, found only here in the New Testament. It recalls the law against yoking unlike animals. The command has been applied to marriage, business partnerships, and religious alliances; its context points first to participation in idolatry and to alliances with those who oppose the gospel.

Naos, temple, specifically the sanctuary, the inner dwelling of the deity, rather than the whole temple complex. Paul uses it of the Christian community (also 1 Corinthians 3:16) and of the believer's body (1 Corinthians 6:19). In a city of temples, the claim that God's true sanctuary was a group of ordinary believers was startling.

christ: The day of salvation that Paul announces is the day that has dawned in Christ, whose death and resurrection chapter 5 has just described. Verse 2 quotes a passage from Isaiah's Servant Songs, where God answers and helps his servant; the New Testament reads those songs as fulfilled in Jesus, and Paul now extends the servant's time of favor to all who hear. The pattern of Paul's life in verses 8-10, "dying, and yet we live on", and "poor, yet making many rich", mirrors Christ's own, who though rich became poor so that others might become rich (8:9). The question "What harmony is there between Christ and Belial?" sets Christ against the powers of evil, and the promise that God will dwell with his people finds its fulfillment in the Son, through whom God makes his people his temple.

hard.q: Does "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers" mean Christians must avoid friendships or marriages with non-Christians?
hard.a:
The verse has often been applied to marriage, and many churches teach on that basis that believers should marry only believers, a principle that 1 Corinthians 7:39 states more directly for widows who remarry. But the context here is wider and more specific. Paul's examples are righteousness and wickedness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, the temple of God and idols. His concern is partnership that draws believers into idolatry or makes them share in unbelief.

The same Paul insisted that believers should not withdraw from the world (1 Corinthians 5:9-10), urged those already married to unbelievers to stay if the spouse was willing (1 Corinthians 7:12-14), and himself ate with and befriended pagans in order to win them (1 Corinthians 9:19-23). Christians differ on how widely to apply the command to business partnerships and other alliances. Most agree that it does not forbid friendship, kindness, or ordinary social life with unbelievers, but calls believers to refuse any bond that would require them to divide their loyalty to Christ.

questions: Paul says it is possible to receive God's grace in vain. What might that look like in the life of someone who has heard the gospel many times?
Which of the paradoxes in verses 8-10 most challenges how you measure a successful or faithful life?
Paul tells the Corinthians that it is their affection, not his, that is restrained. What closes our hearts to people who have loved us honestly?
